transcript:
Meeting: Argus Logistics 
Date: 2026-09-07 16:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Fernandez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Argus, Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Argus, VP Eng), Jorge Martinez (Argus, Security/Infra)

Summary:
- Intro and high level ask: understand unit economics for user-facing chat vs. background summarization workloads and decide between hosted, dedicated, or private deployments.
- Argus has a hard monthly inference budget (~$25k) and wants serious latency SLOs for chat (target 120-200ms p95).
- Discussed batching, KV/prefix cache, quantization, routing to lower-cost model variants, and dedicated pool sizing.
- Agreed next steps: Redwood to send cost model spreadsheet and plan a 1-week benchmark comparing hosted vs. dedicated.

Topics covered:
- Current stack & constraints (traffic, token mix, timelines)
- Per-token cost math and breakpoints for dedicated reservations
- Batching and cache levers to reduce effective token cost
- Security/residency concerns for private deployment
- Pilot scope and success criteria

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros real quick, then Luca will cover how we think about cost levers.
[00:20] Priya: Hi Maya, Priya here. We run the recommendation and chat layer for Argus. We saw Redwood at a conference and want to understand cost side before a pilot.
[00:32] Tom: Tom from eng, mostly here for capacity/ops questions.
[00:35] Jorge: Jorge, security/infra. I'll focus on network and compliance.
[00:40] Maya: Great, Luca?
[00:42] Luca: Thanks. I want to ground the conversation with a quick framing: when customers come to us they often have two different workload profiles — low-latency interactive chat and high-volume async jobs like summarization or vector embedding pipelines. Both drive token consumption differently and the optimal hosting mix can be hybrid.
[01:05] Priya: Exactly, our chat is user-facing — low token lengths per request but strict latency. The summarization jobs are larger tokens but background, can be batched.
[01:18] Luca: Perfect. Can you share rough numbers? average tokens per chat turn, and monthly tokens?
[01:25] Priya: Ballpark — chat average 120 tokens per turn, about 2 million chat requests / month so ~240M tokens. Summarization: 10k jobs/month, average 1.5k tokens = 15M tokens. So total ~255M tokens / month.
[01:48] Maya: Thanks, that helps. Budget?
[01:51] Tom: Our budget top line is $25k/mo for inference at first; we can stretch if ROI is clear but need to be efficient.
[01:58] Maya: Great — that immediately sets a target, that's one of the reasons we look at batching and caching to shrink effective token spend.
[02:08] Luca: Quick mental model: hosted per-token is straightforward — you pay per token served; for dedicated you reserve capacity (monthly commit) and the per-token is amortized lower but you pay upfront for GPUs. Private adds infra/ops costs and often higher fixed fees for support and compliance.
[02:30] Priya: We're most interested in a hybrid where chat is hosted or dedicated depending on latency and summarization maybe runs on reserved pools or even on- prem if private is needed.
[02:40] Jorge: Key security ask — we need SOC 2, audit logs, and KMS integration for keys. If private, we want to manage KMS on our side. Can Redwood do that?
[02:51] Luca: Yes — private deployments support customer-managed KMS, and hosted supports encrypted at rest with our keys and optional customer-managed keys for enterprise. We'll share the private-deploy checklist.
[03:05] Tom: On latency — you mentioned 120-200ms p95 target for chat. Is that realistic on hosted for a 120-token turn?
[03:13] Luca: Depends on model size and region. For a 7B equivalent optimized model we routinely see 80-150ms p95 on hosted with our lowest-lossy quantization and dynamic batching disabled for the lowest latency; dedicated pools let you pin and reduce jitter further. The important levers: model variant (7B vs 13B), quantization profile, batch policy, and KV/prefix cache hit rate.
[03:39] Priya: Can you elaborate on KV/prefix cache? Our chat has a lot of repeated system tokens & repeated context for known customers.
[03:47] Luca: Sure. Prefix caching stores the KV cache for repeated prefixes so subsequent calls need fewer compute tokens; for chat this can drop per-request compute by 20-40% if you get high cache hit rates. For Argus, if your system prompt + initial customer history is 60% stable, you might effectively shave token compute by ~25% on chat. We also do automatic prefix detection to avoid manual engineering.
[04:12] Tom: What about batching tradeoffs? We care about latency.
[04:15] Luca: There's a spectrum. Continuous small batching can improve throughput and reduce per-token cost but adds latency. For background summarization we batch aggressively (large batch sizes, better utilization). For chat we use micro-batching and target upper bounds that keep p95 under your target. Dedicated pools let you scale concurrency without affecting other tenants.
[04:35] Priya: Pricing math — can you walk through an example? Say 240M chat tokens, 15M summary tokens, $25k budget.
[04:45] Maya: Luca, want to run a quick scenario?
[04:47] Luca: Sure. For hosted, using our reference 7B gen price of $0.0006 per input token and $0.0012 per output token — rough example — if chat is symmetric input/output and counts as one token type, you'd get to, say, $0.0009 effective average per token. At 255M tokens that's about $229.5k/mo — so too high. But that's naive without caching/batching.
[05:12] Priya: Ok that's an order of magnitude over budget.
[05:15] Luca: Right. Now apply levers: prefix caching reduces compute by 25%, that drops the effective token count to ~191M. Then use batching for summarization (we can run large batches overnight) which reduces cost for that slice by about 60% relative to worst-case. Also you can route lower-criticality requests to smaller, quantized variants — e.g., 7B-quantized at lower cost for non-sensitive summarization. With those levers we could potentially drop cost by 3-4x.
[05:46] Tom: So roughly, you'd expect $229.5k / 3.5 ~ $65k. Still above $25k. Where does dedicated help?
[05:56] Luca: Dedicated is where reserved GPU pools change the equation. If you commit to a pool sized for your throughput we can amortize cost and lower per-token realized price. For example, a reserved 8 x A10s-equivalent pool with expected utilization could drop per-token to something in the $0.0002-$0.00035 effective range after utilization and caching. But that assumes high sustained utilization — if use is spiky you either pay for unused reserved capacity or we add burst capacity.
[06:26] Priya: We can commit to a minimum if the numbers make sense. What are typical commit sizes?
[06:29] Maya: We have tiered reserved offerings — monthly committed GPU-hours equivalency. We'll put together a few right-sized scenarios based on your 255M tokens and desired p95. We'll show break-even points between hosted and dedicated.
[06:42] Jorge: For private deployment, what are the incremental costs? We're interested only if we need VPC/on-prem for compliance.
[06:49] Luca: Private includes a platform fee and ops support; customers also cover infra. Typical pattern: private is more expensive in headcount/ops but gives you total control over keys and network. If you need customer-managed KMS and air-gap, that's the route. In some cases, customers combine — they run private for sensitive workloads and hosted/dedicated for the rest.
[07:08] Priya: Ok. A couple technical questions — quantization: does Redwood support 4-bit int quantization or 8-bit? We're concerned about quality degradation for chat.
[07:18] Luca: We support multiple quantization profiles. 8-bit often yields negligible quality delta for many tasks; 4-bit can be disruptive for some models but works okay for embeddings and non-critical summarization. We'll include quantization/quality guidance tied to your prompt set in the spreadsheet.
[07:33] Tom: About fallbacks — if a dedicated pool is saturated, is there an automatic fallback to hosted so we don't lose traffic?
[07:40] Maya: Yes — smart routing lets you fall back to hosted variants when dedicated is saturated. You can set policies by SLA; critical traffic can hit higher-cost paths but remain available. That helps avoid overcommitting reserved capacity for rare spikes.
[07:53] Priya: What about observability and per-route cost breakdowns? We need to attribute costs to product lines.
[07:59] Luca: Redwood Console provides token-level breakdown by route/model, latency histograms, and cost attribution. For dedicated, we also expose utilization dashboards. We'll share screenshots in the follow-up.
[08:12] Jorge: Networking — VPC peering or private endpoint? Egress bandwidth limits? We have strict egress caps and prefer peering where possible.
[08:20] Luca: For private we support VPC peering and private endpoints. Hosted can do private connectivity via secure egress and IB connections in some regions — we'll need your infra diagram to confirm. We'll ask for expected egress and any proxy constraints.
[08:33] Tom: Pilot proposal — can we run a 1-week benchmark: 3 days hosted run, 3 days dedicated reserved pool sized to expected peak, compare latency and cost?
[08:43] Maya: That's common. Luca will define test prompts, harness, and pass/fail criteria. We typically calibrate to p95 and cost per 1k requests.
[08:52] Priya: Success criteria for us: chat p95 <= 200ms, total monthly extrapolated cost <= $25k with caching and dedicated assumptions, and no data residency or KMS roadblock.
[09:05] Luca: Noted. We'll simulate cache hit rates at 20/30/50% to show sensitivity.
[09:11] Priya: One more — SLA expectations. If we do dedicated, do we get formal latency SLOs?
[09:16] Maya: Yes, there's SLA tiers for Dedicated with uptime and latency commitments. The higher SLA tier includes faster incident response and credits for breaches. We'll include SLA options and uplift pricing.
[09:26] Tom: Any recommended models? We're trying to balance quality vs cost.
[09:30] Luca: For chat, 7B-13B family depending on hallucination tolerance. For Argus we recommend starting with an efficient 7B optimized + prefix caching for chat; move to 13B for high-value flows. For summarization, a quantized 7B or even dedicated CPU/quant pipeline might be fine.
[09:47] Priya: Can we get a concrete example of break-even?
[09:50] Luca: We'll produce scenarios in the spreadsheet. Example quick one: if you have 255M tokens and achieve 30% cache + 50% batching benefit on background tasks and commit to a reserved pool at 70% utilization, you may get to ~ $20-30k equivalent monthly — that's why we need the exact traffic pattern.
[10:12] Maya: We'll send the spreadsheet with toggles for cache hit, batching, model mix, and reserved pool sizes.
[10:18] Jorge: From security perspective, we need SOC 2, KMS, and SIEM forwarding. Also minimum data retention logs — can Redwood provide audit logs to our SIEM?
[10:27] Luca: Yes — audit logs plus optional log forwarding. For private we can ship logs directly into your SIEM. For hosted we provide secure exports.
[10:35] Priya: Ok let's recap next steps.
[10:38] Maya: Recap: 1) Redwood sends per-token spreadsheet and model/quantization guidance; 2) Argus provides sample prompt mix and infra diagram; 3) Redwood proposes a 1-week benchmark plan comparing hosted vs dedicated; 4) Jorge intro to Redwood infra lead for VPC specs.
[10:55] Tom: Sounds good. timeline?
[10:58] Maya: We'll aim to send the spreadsheet and pilot plan by 2026-09-10 so infra alignment can happen before the engineering week starting 2026-09-20.
[11:08] Priya: Perfect. Thanks all.
[11:10] Jorge: Thanks.
[11:12] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with the attachments.
